prompt: In the closest-pair algorithm, δ is the smallest distance found within either half. For each point in the strip (sorted by y), why is it enough to compare it with only the next 7 points?

options.text: Because the strip contains at most 8 points in total
options.explanation: The strip can contain almost all n points. The bound is per point: few points can sit close *above* any given point.

options.text: Because 7 is a heuristic that works on random data but can fail
options.explanation: It is a proven bound, not a heuristic. The packing argument holds for any input of distinct points.

options.text: Because the recursion guarantees each half contains at most 7 points
options.explanation: Halves shrink only to the base case of 2 or 3 points at the bottom; at the top each half holds half the n points.

options.text: Because points more than 7 positions apart in y order cannot be strictly closer than δ
options.explanation: Correct. A closer partner must lie in a box δ tall and 2δ wide above the point. Partition each recursive half’s part of the box into four δ/2 squares, assigning split-line ties to their original half. Each square holds at most one point from that half, since two would be closer than δ. So beyond 7 neighbours in y order, nothing can be closer than δ.

workedExample:
1. Any pair closer than δ that straddles the line must have both points within δ of the line.
2. Fix a point p in the strip. A closer partner q above p has a y-coordinate between p's y and that plus δ, and an x-coordinate within δ of the line: a rectangle δ tall and 2δ wide.
3. Cut the rectangle into a 2 × 4 grid of squares with side δ/2. A small square's diagonal is about 0.71δ, shorter than δ.
4. Same-half points are at least δ apart, so no small square can hold two points of the same half. Applying the four squares on each side to that side's points (with points on the line assigned to their own half), each half contributes at most four points.
5. That's at most 8 points in the rectangle including p, so at most 7 others to check.

Because the strip scan is linear, the recursion keeps merge sort's shape: two half-size calls plus linear work, giving O(n log n) for n points.
